content: The appropriate use of diagnostic tests is critical for the effective management of suspected influenza cases. Ensuring the availability and proper utilization of influenza diagnostic tests is essential to improve access to antiviral medications, particularly during the early stages of the disease. Healthcare systems must develop expertise in selecting and implementing diagnostic tests that are most suitable for their specific settings. For further details, refer to the recommendations on diagnostics in Section 10. It is important to consider the influence of community prevalence of influenza viruses on diagnostic testing. When influenza viruses are circulating at high prevalence within a community, most patients with positive nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) will indeed have influenza. However, some patients with negative results may also have the disease. Conversely, when influenza viruses are circulating at low prevalence or are not circulating at all, most patients with negative test results will not have influenza, but a small number of patients with positive results may also not have the disease. This pattern is also observed with influenza digital immunoassay (DIA) tests. Alternative strategies, such as conducting polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing and delaying treatment until results are available, face significant feasibility and acceptability challenges. Treating all patients without testing would result in a substantial proportion of individuals receiving unnecessary treatment, especially in low-prevalence settings. This could lead to overuse of antiviral medications, such as baloxavir (a WHO-recommended treatment), increasing the risk of antimicrobial resistance and exposing patients to unnecessary adverse events. On the other hand, not treating any patients would result in individuals with influenza experiencing slightly longer durations of illness, which would represent a significant proportion of the population in high-prevalence settings. The conditional recommendation reflects the low certainty of evidence regarding the relative impact of testing strategies on patient-important outcomes. The differences in outcomes across strategies are likely to be very small. However, the Guideline Development Group (GDG) noted that if more effective treatments were available, the impact on quality-adjusted life days (QALDs) might be affected. This recommendation is preferred over alternatives such as treating all patients, treating no patients, or conducting PCR testing and waiting for results to determine whether antiviral treatment should be administered. The interpretation of test results should account for the prevalence of influenza viruses circulating in the community (high or low prevalence) as part of the pre-testing probability of disease. Influenza NAATs and DIAs are most accurate when upper respiratory tract specimens are collected within 3–4 days of symptom onset. Collecting high-quality upper respiratory tract specimens from patients with suspected influenza is crucial. Nasopharyngeal specimens, either swabs or aspirates, yield the highest detection rates for influenza viruses. High yields can also be achieved by testing combined nasal and throat swab specimens, collected separately and placed together in the same sterile specimen container. Proper interpretation of test results, particularly negative results from influenza DIAs, is important due to the potential for false negatives during periods of high influenza prevalence. This is especially critical for patients with suspected non-severe influenza who are at high risk of progression to severe disease. Patients with negative upper respiratory tract specimens by influenza NAAT but with lower respiratory tract disease may still have influenza virus replication in the lower respiratory tract. In such cases, testing lower respiratory specimens (e.g., sputum, endotracheal aspirates from intubated patients, or bronchoalveolar lavage fluid) using influenza NAAT can provide valuable information for clinical management. The PCR-wait strategy, compared to the Treat none strategy, offered 23,337 symptom-free days per 100,000 population but was associated with an additional 501 adverse events per 100,000 population. The PCR-treat strategy mirrored the outcomes of the Treat all strategy, as a full regimen of baloxavir (a single dose) was administered upfront before receiving test results. Both strategies were associated with a QALD loss compared to the Treat none strategy due to the highest number of adverse events. NAATs, including RT-PCR, are molecular assays that detect influenza virus nucleic acids in respiratory specimens with high sensitivity and specificity. In inpatient settings, NAATs may be associated with a small increase in QALDs. Currently, oseltamivir is the only antiviral recommended for use in severe influenza patients. Its effect on mortality and ICU admission is uncertain, though it may reduce hospitalization days. The differences in QALDs across treatment strategies are very small. The GDG inferred that the marginal increase in QALDs for the NAAT and PCR-treat strategies was preferable to the Treat all strategy. Targeted clinical treatment is preferred to avoid wasting resources, overusing antivirals (contrary to antimicrobial stewardship strategies), and unnecessarily exposing patients to adverse events. The GDG also noted that the availability of a more effective antiviral in the future could impact the model's output on QALDs. Influenza NAATs and other molecular assays may not be widely available in many clinical settings due to their cost. Access to influenza diagnostics is essential for guiding treatment decisions, particularly for targeted treatments of viral pneumonias such as influenza or COVID-19. Ensuring diagnostic results are available within a timeframe that can guide treatment is critical for implementation. Administering treatment with oseltamivir as soon as practical requires appropriate use of diagnostic tests.
